U.S. states increasingly require identification to vote – an ostensive attempt to deter fraud that prompts complaints of selective disenfranchisement. Using a difference-in-differences design on a 1.6-billion-observations panel dataset, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation. These results hold through a large number of specifications. Our most demanding specification controls for state, year, and voter fixed effects, along with state and voter time-varying controls. Based on this specification, we obtain point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for effects both on overall registration and turnout (with 95 percent confidence intervals of [-2.3; 2.1pp] and [-3.0; 2.8pp], respectively), and +1.4pp for the effect on the turnout of non-white voters relative to whites (with a 95 percent confidence interval of [-0.5; 3.2pp]). The lack of negative impact on voter turnout cannot be attributed to voters’ reaction against the laws, measured by campaign contributions and self-reported political engagement. However, the likelihood that non-white voters were contacted by a campaign increases by 4.7 percentage points, suggesting that parties’ mobilization might have offset modest effects of the laws on the participation of ethnic minorities. Finally, strict ID requirements have no effect on fraud – actual or perceived. Overall, our findings suggest that efforts to improve elections may be better directed at other reforms.

U.S. states increasingly require identification to vote – an ostensive attempt to deter fraud that prompts complaints of selective disenfranchisement. Using a difference-in-differences design on a 1.6-billion-observations panel dataset, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation. These results hold through a large number of specifications. Our most demanding specification controls for state, year, and voter fixed effects, along with state and voter time-varying controls. Based on this specification, we obtain point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for effects both on overall registration and turnout (with 95 percent confidence intervals of [-2.3; 2.1pp] and [-3.0; 2.8pp], respectively), and +1.4pp for the effect on the turnout of non-white voters relative to whites (with a 95 percent confidence interval of [-0.5; 3.2pp]). The lack of negative impact on voter turnout cannot be attributed to voters’ reaction against the laws, measured by campaign contributions and self-reported political engagement. However, the likelihood that non-white voters were contacted by a campaign increases by 4.7 percentage points, suggesting that parties’ mobilization might have offset modest effects of the laws on the participation of ethnic minorities. Finally, strict ID requirements have no effect on fraud – actual or perceived. Overall, our findings suggest that efforts to improve elections may be better directed at other reforms.

The presidential election of 2000 and the highly controversial recount in Florida brought the term “voter confidence” into the political lexicon. However, the rhetorical pull of the term “voter confidence” is much stronger than proof of any actual empirical relationship between voter confidence and voter turnout.
This explainer was last updated on May 13, 2026.
Introduction
In the summer of 2001, the National Commission on Federal Election Reform issued its report, To Ensure Pride and Confidence in American Elections (http://web1.millercenter.org/commissions/comm_2001.pdf). Seven years later, when the U.S. Supreme Court (https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/07pdf/07-21.pdf)decided in Crawford v. Marion County Board of Elections that strict photo voter ID laws were constitutional, Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that “public confidence in the integrity of the electoral process has independent significance because it encourages citizen participation in the democratic process.” In the aftermath of the 2020 elections, many state legislatures considered a variety of restrictive election laws, including in Georgia. In the remarks he made after signing SB 202, Governor Brian Kemp stated (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1szW8XH2mrw), "There’s no doubt there were many alarming issues with how the election was handled, and those problems understandably led to a crisis of confidence in the ballot box here in Georgia."
Viewing voter confidence as a measure of the quality of American elections and assuming that it is linked to the willingness of Americans to vote are intuitively appealing. However, research finds only a weak causal connection between voter confidence and voter turnout—it has not found clear causal evidence that certain high-profile election administration practices, such as voter ID laws, affect voter confidence.
Surveys have measured public opinion about voter confidence for over two decades. The strongest influence on voter confidence in such surveys, regardless of how the question is asked, is whether the candidate one supports has won or lost an election. This is known as the “winner-loser effect (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1089/elj.2022.0055).”Beyond this phenomenon, voter confidence has been found to be influenced to a lesser degree by other factors, including the intensity of partisan competition and the experience of casting ballots.
Measuring Confidence
When measuring anything, it's important to consider what exact concept is being measured and whether the measurement approach actually captures it. When we try to measure the confidence of voters, we need to ask exactly what they're confident about: that the election was fair? That the votes were counted as they were cast?
When political scientists study voter confidence, they ask voters some variant of the question, “Do you believe that votes in the most recent election were counted as cast?” This question focuses on the mechanics of marking a ballot and having it counted accurately, which is narrower than asking whether the last election was fair—and asking whether the last election was fair is narrower than asking whether “elections in America are usually fair.”
Within this specific academic context, answers about voter confidence are fairly consistent regardless of the precise wording of the question. However, there is one important exception to this pattern of consistency: when survey respondents are asked about their confidence in the parts of the electoral process with which they have direct contact, such as their own vote, they are much more confident than when asked about parts of the electoral process they have indirect contact with, such as the process in the nation as a whole. One consequence of this is that in political debates involving voter confidence, it is possible to cherry-pick survey research in support of arguments that voters either have high levels of confidence in American politics or do not.
Here's an example of how degrees of voter confidence vary with the degree of direct voter contact with the process. In the MIT module of the 2020 Cooperative Election Study (https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/QNZ3F2) (CES), respondents were asked the following question before the election: “How confident are you that your vote in the General Election will be as you intend?” They were also asked, “How confident are you that votes in [your county/your state/nationwide] will be counted as voters intend?” The response categories were very confident, somewhat confident, not too confident, not at all confident, and don’t know.
Looking at the responses to these questions (Figure 1), two patterns immediately jump out. First, regardless of the target of the question (“your vote,” the “local vote,” etc.), confidence was greater after the election than before. For instance, the percentage of voters who said they were very confident their vote would be counted as they intended was 38% before the election, but this jumped to 61% when asked after the election.
Figure 1 shows levels of voter confidence before and after the 2020 general election. These “levels” are “very confident”, “somewhat confident”, “not too confident”, “not at all confident”, and “don’t know.” The graph displays voter confidence across several stages: confidence that votes were counted accurately in their local area, in their state, and nationwide, as well as confidence that their own vote was counted correctly.

Figure 1 shows levels of voter confidence before and after the 2020 general election. These “levels” are “very confident”, “somewhat confident”, “not too confident”, “not at all confident”, and “don’t know.” The graph displays voter confidence across several stages: confidence that votes were counted accurately in their local area, in their state, and nationwide, as well as confidence that their own vote was counted correctly.
Second, confidence was greatest—both before and after the election—as the target of the question got closer to the voter. For instance, while 38% of respondents overall were very confident their own vote would be counted as intended in the pre-election survey, 35% were very confident that votes would be counted as intended in their own county or community. These percentages dropped to 29% and 15% when the question asked about the state and the nation, respectively.
Questions about the mechanical aspects of voting tend to elicit more optimistic responses in public-opinion surveys than vague questions about the honesty of elections. For instance, immediately before the 2016 election, the Gallup organization (http://news.gallup.com/poll/196976/update-americans-confidence-voting-election.aspx) asked respondents, “How confident are you that, across the country, the votes will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election?” To this question, 69% responded that they were either very or somewhat confident. However, the poll also asked about how much confidence they had in the “honesty of elections.” Here, only 30% answered that they were confident.
Looking at more recent data, these trends remain. After the 2024 presidential election, the 2024 Survey of the Performance of American Elections (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/projects/survey-performance-american-elections) asked respondents to answer the same voter confidence questions as the 2020 CES MIT module, and the results were unsurprising given the previous years’ data. Nearly 70% of respondents said that they were “very confident” that their own vote was counted as intended in 2024, and this proportion decreased as respondents were asked about their confidence in the vote-counting process in their county/city, state, and nationwide.
Figure 2 shows levels of voter confidence after the 2024 general election. These “levels” are “very confident”, “somewhat confident”, “not too confident”, “not at all confident”, and “don’t know.” The graph displays voter confidence across several stages: confidence that votes were counted accurately in their local area, in their state, and nationwide, as well as confidence that their own vote was counted correctly.

Confidence and outcomes
We've already seen that answers to voter-confidence survey questions vary as the target of the question changes. What else affects voter confidence? The main answer points us in two directions related to political outcomes—who wins, and how close elections are.
The “winner-loser effect” is illustrated by the changing answers to voter confidence questions since they were first asked in 2000. Figure 3 shows the percentage of respondents who reported they were very confident their vote was counted as intended in the Survey of the Performance of American Elections, which was conducted immediately after the 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections. The data for prior elections shows the percentages taken from commercial public opinion polls and reported in research by Michael Sances and Charles Stewart III (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.electstud.2015.08.004).
Figure 3 shows the proportion of respondents who said they were “very confident” that their vote was counted as intended from 2000 to 2024. The x-axis is the year, and the y-axis is the proportion. The overall proportion for these years is shown along with the party breakdown for Democrats and Republicans.
Note: Data from 2008-2024 are from the Survey of the Performance of American Elections (https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/SPAE)

In the first two elections, Republicans were more likely by a margin of 20 percentage points to say they were confident that their vote was counted as intended. The relative opinions of Democrats and Republicans switched in 2008 and became even more entrenched in 2012. Republican confidence rebounded in 2016 while Democratic confidence sagged.
All the major changes in confidence correspond with changes in the parties’ electoral fortunes. This pattern held in 2020, but we observed the largest partisan gap to date at 32 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans. This can likely be attributed to President Trump’s attempts to cast doubt on the results. (Surveyed Republicans cited Trump as their primary source for believing fraud occurred (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/republicans-belief-voter-fraud-opinion-poll/)). In 2024, this partisan gap dramatically shrank as the percentage of very confident Republicans increased by about 20 percentage points and the percentage of very confident Democrats decreased by more than 10 percentage points. This is likely due to Republicans feeling more confident about elections after President Trump won and Democrats experiencing a dip in trust after Harris lost. According to a report by the Yankelovich Center at UCSD (https://yankelovichcenter.ucsd.edu/_files/reports/How-Did-Trust-in-Elections-Change-After-the-2024-Presidential-Contest_.pdf), the narrowing of this partisan gap was mostly driven by higher levels of trust among Republican voters after the 2024 election. Despite increased party polarization, notice that the overall average level of voter confidence has not changed very much across the past six elections.
Voter confidence is also influenced by the sniping that goes on between candidates in the heat of their campaigns. In a close contest, it's common for both sides to accuse the other of dirty tricks. The effects of such attacks are evident when we asked respondents whether votes in their own state were counted as intended. Figure 4 shows the percentage of voters who were very confident that their own states’ votes were counted as intended in the 2024 presidential election on the y-axis, and the percentage share of the vote for Harris on the x-axis. The two lines display the relationship between the points in states that Harris lost (left) and Harris won (right), respectively. Note that regardless of the winner, the closer the elections are (proximity to 50% on the x-axis), the less confident voters are in the result.
Figure 4 compares the proportion of votes for Kamala Harris with the proportion of respondents who said they were “very confident” that their vote was counted as intended in 2024. Each state is represented as a point. The x-axis is the state-level proportion of votes for Harris, and the y-axis is the proportion of “very confident” respondents in that state. Two lines are drawn to show the trend for states that Harris won and states that Harris lost.

Confidence and administration
It's common to justify election reforms by arguing they will increase voter confidence in the electoral system. However, there's little evidence that election administration has a direct effect on voter confidence. The major exception to this statement is that voters who experience problems at polling places tend to be less confident than voters who don’t.
The issue of voter confidence and election reforms has been front and center in justifications for stricter voter ID laws. (If you want to read more about this issue in detail, please see our Voter ID explainer (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification).) As noted above, Justice Stevens’s decision justifying the constitutionality of strict voter ID laws in Crawford v. Marion County Board of Elections credited Indiana’s argument that strict voter ID laws could increase voter confidence. However, subsequent research on this question by Stephen Ansolabehere (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/effects-of-identification-requirements-on-votingevidence-from-the-experiences-of-voters-on-electionday/7E19799BF65B5E1AA38BCC3EB9BD83A7), Shaun Bowler (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261379415000062), Nathaniel Persily (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults), and Charles Stewart III (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stflr68&div=38&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals) reveals no correlation between the adoption of strict voter ID laws and increases in voter confidence (Ansolabehere 2009 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/effects-of-identification-requirements-on-votingevidence-from-the-experiences-of-voters-on-electionday/7E19799BF65B5E1AA38BCC3EB9BD83A7); Ansolabehere and Persily 2007 (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults); Bowler et al. 2015 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261379415000062); (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults)Stewart et al. 2016 (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stflr68&div=38&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals)). Indeed, if anything, the political climate created by debates about strict ID laws could actually be reducing confidence and further polarizing opinions along partisan lines, according to studies by Shaun Bowler and Todd Donovan (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/abs/partisan-model-of-electoral-reform-voter-identification-laws-and-confidence-in-state-elections/73433AA2DA6926F9B794A2DDEA0F0494) in 2021 and Lonna Atkeson (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ssqu.12110) in 2014.
Voter confidence is also influenced by a voter’s general experience with the administrative process; a positive encounter for a voter reinforces their trust in the system. This pattern held in 2020, but we observed the largest partisan gap to date at 32 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans. This can likely be attributed to President Trump’s attempts to cast doubt on the results. (Surveyed Republicans cited Trump as their primary source for believing fraud occurred (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/republicans-belief-voter-fraud-opinion-poll/)). In 2024, this partisan gap dramatically shrank as the percentage of very confident Republicans increased by about 20 percentage points and the percentage of very confident Democrats decreased by more than 10 percentage points. This is likely due to Republicans feeling more confident about elections after President Trump won and Democrats experiencing a dip in trust after Harris lost. According to a report by the Yankelovich Center at UCSD (https://yankelovichcenter.ucsd.edu/_files/reports/How-Did-Trust-in-Elections-Change-After-the-2024-Presidential-Contest_.pdf), the narrowing of this partisan gap was mostly driven by higher levels of trust among Republican voters after the 2024 election. Despite increased party polarization, notice that the overall average level of voter confidence has not changed very much across the past six elections.
Voter confidence is also influenced by the sniping that goes on between candidates in the heat of their campaigns. In a close contest, it's common for both sides to accuse the other of dirty tricks. The effects of such attacks are evident when we asked respondents whether votes in their own state were counted as intended. Figure 4 shows the percentage of voters who were very confident that their own states’ votes were counted as intended in the 2024 presidential election on the y-axis, and the percentage share of the vote for Harris on the x-axis. The two lines display the relationship between the points in states that Harris lost (left) and Harris won (right), respectively. Note that regardless of the winner, the closer the elections are (proximity to 50% on the x-axis), the less confident voters are in the result.
Figure 4 compares the proportion of votes for Kamala Harris with the proportion of respondents who said they were “very confident” that their vote was counted as intended in 2024. Each state is represented as a point. The x-axis is the state-level proportion of votes for Harris, and the y-axis is the proportion of “very confident” respondents in that state. Two lines are drawn to show the trend for states that Harris won and states that Harris lost.

Confidence and administration
It's common to justify election reforms by arguing they will increase voter confidence in the electoral system. However, there's little evidence that election administration has a direct effect on voter confidence. The major exception to this statement is that voters who experience problems at polling places tend to be less confident than voters who don’t.
The issue of voter confidence and election reforms has been front and center in justifications for stricter voter ID laws. (If you want to read more about this issue in detail, please see our Voter ID explainer (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification).) As noted above, Justice Stevens’s decision justifying the constitutionality of strict voter ID laws in Crawford v. Marion County Board of Elections credited Indiana’s argument that strict voter ID laws could increase voter confidence. However, subsequent research on this question by Stephen Ansolabehere (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/effects-of-identification-requirements-on-votingevidence-from-the-experiences-of-voters-on-electionday/7E19799BF65B5E1AA38BCC3EB9BD83A7), Shaun Bowler (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261379415000062), Nathaniel Persily (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults), and Charles Stewart III (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stflr68&div=38&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals) reveals no correlation between the adoption of strict voter ID laws and increases in voter confidence (Ansolabehere 2009 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/effects-of-identification-requirements-on-votingevidence-from-the-experiences-of-voters-on-electionday/7E19799BF65B5E1AA38BCC3EB9BD83A7); Ansolabehere and Persily 2007 (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults); Bowler et al. 2015 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261379415000062); (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults)Stewart et al. 2016 (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stflr68&div=38&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals)). A search for academic and advocacy research pieces on voter fraud in California since the 2020 election cycle involved
multiple search tools, including Google, Google Scholar, journal databases (such as those available on the California
State Library’s online resources webpage), university-adjacent research organizations (such as Harvard University’s
Electoral Integrity Project), all 58 counties’ Grand Jury websites, and ChatGPT.
Searches utilized key terms, such as “election fraud,” “voter fraud,” or “election integrity,” which were identified as
common terms used in research relevant to this topic. Searches were filtered such that research on elections prior to
2020 were not included. Additionally, research that was topic-adjacent, but with no specific analysis or findings related
to voter fraud (ex: a Grand Jury report talking about observations of the electoral process and commending county
staff), was excluded.

A search for academic and advocacy research pieces on voter fraud in California since the 2020 election cycle involved
multiple search tools, including Google, Google Scholar, journal databases (such as those available on the California
State Library’s online resources webpage), university-adjacent research organizations (such as Harvard University’s
Electoral Integrity Project), all 58 counties’ Grand Jury websites, and ChatGPT.
Searches utilized key terms, such as “election fraud,” “voter fraud,” or “election integrity,” which were identified as
common terms used in research relevant to this topic. Searches were filtered such that research on elections prior to
2020 were not included. Additionally, research that was topic-adjacent, but with no specific analysis or findings related
to voter fraud (ex: a Grand Jury report talking about observations of the electoral process and commending county
staff), was excluded.

Study Reveals the Lasting Voter Suppression Effects of ... https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/study-reveals-lasting-voter-suppression-effects-restrictive-texas-law # Study Reveals the Lasting Voter Suppression Effects of Restrictive Texas Law New research shows that a restrictive voting law in Texas made people less likely to vote for at least two years after having a mail ballot application or ballot rejected. ... Brennan Center **research** has already shown that thousands of mail ballot applications and mail ballots were rejected during the 2022 primary due to S.B. 1 and that nonwhite voters were disproportionately impacted. A new working paper from the Brennan Center along with Michael G. Miller and Ian Shapiro shows that voters whose applications and ballots were rejected in the primary were considerably less likely to vote in the 2022 general election and the 2024 primary. ## Research on voter ID
Research on this issue is the topic of ongoing scholarly debate, and whether implementing voter ID requirements leads to a decrease in racial minority turnout is still open to dispute.
Some scholars have found a decrease in racial minority turnout nationwide, but other studies have found no effect of voter ID laws on racial minority turnout, and some have even found an *increase* in youth turnout.
Beyond minority turnout, the effect of voter ID laws on turnout generally is also unclear.
Some studies examined this relationship and found no statistical association between strict ID laws and decreased turnout (Ansolabehere, 2009 and Mycoff et al, 2009).
However, work by the GAO has shown a negative correlation between strict photo ID laws and turnout.
This finding has been supported by other research (Kuk et al, 2020 and Darrah-Okike et al, 2020).
Debate continues, since there are methodological challenges to estimating the true causal effects of strict voter identification law, including deficiencies in data quality and sensitivity of results to choices made in statistical estimation (Erikson and Minnite, 2009 and Grimmer et al, 2018).

Research on this issue is the topic of ongoing scholarly debate, and whether implementing voter ID requirements leads to a decrease in racial minority turnout is still open to dispute.
Some scholars have found a decrease in racial minority turnout nationwide, but other studies have found no effect of voter ID laws on racial minority turnout, and some have even found an *increase* in youth turnout.
Beyond minority turnout, the effect of voter ID laws on turnout generally is also unclear.
Some studies examined this relationship and found no statistical association between strict ID laws and decreased turnout (Ansolabehere, 2009 and Mycoff et al, 2009).
However, work by the GAO has shown a negative correlation between strict photo ID laws and turnout.
This finding has been supported by other research (Kuk et al, 2020 and Darrah-Okike et al, 2020).
Debate continues, since there are methodological challenges to estimating the true causal effects of strict voter identification law, including deficiencies in data quality and sensitivity of results to choices made in statistical estimation (Erikson and Minnite, 2009 and Grimmer et al, 2018).

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: October 15, 2026 at 3:13 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
A healthy democracy depends on both public participation and public trust. Without either, the system risks disaffection and loss of legitimacy.
California has made numerous moves in recent years to boost voter participation. From making it easier than ever to vote by mail to overly-liberal ballot harvesting laws, the Golden State has worked to optimize the public participation component of its election administration.
California has also maintained rising levels of public confidence in aspects of its elections. In 2017, just 47% of likely voters and 40% of adults either had “quite a lot of” or a “great deal of” confidence in how California counts votes, according to surveys by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California. By 2024, those figures rose to 63% and 53%, respectively.
Lurking beneath (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/time-trends-all-adults-1024-corrected.pdf) those 2024 numbers were bigger concerns about election integrity than those figures suggest. The same survey found that 42% of adults and 43% of likely voters said they were “somewhat concerned” or “very concerned” that it’s “too easy for people who are not eligible to vote in California elections.”
Enter Proposition 39.
The proposal seeks to improve public confidence in elections with a simple rule: voters must present a government-issued ID when voting in person or include the last four digits of a government-issued ID that corresponds to identification used at the time of registration on the ballots they intend to mail in. For those who do not have such identification, the measure calls for free identification to be provided for voting.
It also requires election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists and “use best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations. Finally, it directs regular audits by the State Auditor to ensure compliance with these rules and offer recommendations for how to improve election integrity.
There’s nothing radical about these recommendations. Thirty six states require voters to present some form of identification when voting. Such a requirement is commonplace around the world, including in Canada and Mexico. The logic of identification requirements is quite obvious: it’s simply another check to ensure that people are who they say they are when they vote. In fact, poll workers in California already ask (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/trusted-info-voter-id-reg-requirements.pdf) first-time federal election voters who didn’t include an ID number at the time of registration for ID if they show up to the polls.
Opponents of voter identification requirements counter that requiring voters to provide identification at the polls is an unacceptable barrier to democratic participation. We disagree. If people can clear the “barrier” of presenting an ID to buy cigarettes or alcohol or use a credit card or get on an airplane, they can present ID to vote.
Opponents likewise counter that requiring voters to write the last four digits of their ID on their ballots introduces a failure point or privacy risk. We are sympathetic to privacy concerns, though such concerns would be more serious if the rule was to write the total ID number. And the failure point is real — what if voters write the wrong numbers? — but fixable. Ballots can be cured.
Research on the impact of such rules has been mixed over the years, with one review published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2019 finding (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) that “strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.” Echoing this is an analysis published (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) by the journal Research & Politics in December 2024 which found “no compelling evidence that strict voter ID laws consistently suppress or boost voter turnout. Rather, the modest and opposing impacts across contexts appear to net out to minimal aggregate effects on participation, consistent with research showing that electoral reforms often produce small equilibrium effects.”

What could be the most controversial component of the measure is its mandate that election officials use “best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations using “government data.” The measure does not define these terms, thus giving the state and election officials room to figure out how to do that in the most reasonable manner possible. While this editorial board isn’t of the view that noncitizen voting is rampant, it doesn’t seem irrational to occasionally confirm people who attest to their citizenship actually are citizens.
If passed, we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period as it’s worked out. Combining the convenience of voting with basic verification isn’t voter suppression — it’s just common-sense governance. Vote Yes on Proposition 39.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:04 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.

Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.

Article continues below this ad
“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.

“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.
Table Of Contents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking
California Should Continue to Promote Voter Participation and Improve the Election Process
Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. This and other research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129241283169) suggests this may be because voters view election laws through a partisan lens and their confidence may be more heavily influenced by partisan rhetoric and whether their preferred candidate wins or loses an election. 13 (javascript:void(0)) See Lonna Rae Atkeson, Eli McKown-Dawson, and Robert M.
