Why Voter ID
Our democracy relies on confidence in our elections, but Californians’ trust is fading. Voters are concerned about election security thanks, in part, to issues like unchecked ballot harvesting, lack of citizenship verification, and inconsistent signature reviews. A bombshell report by the non-partisan Transparency Foundation gives California a failing grade on election practices.
"From its failure to maintain accurate voter registration lists to its refusal to verify the identity and eligibility of voters, California by far has the worst election practices in the nation."
-Transparency California
We are launching a transformative campaign, bringing a common-sense constitutional amendment to the 2026 ballot to restore order, fairness, and trust in California’s elections.
The Voter ID Initiative: A Two-Step Solution
The proposed amendment, Proposition 39 , will:
Require Voter ID for Every Ballot Counted: All votes, whether cast in-person or by mail, will be counted only after verification of a government-issued identification.
Citizenship Verification: Require the Secretary of State and county elections officials to use government data to verify citizenship attestations on voter registrations, closing loopholes and protecting voter rolls from error or abuse.
These basic safeguards will not hinder legal voting, but guarantee each valid vote is protected.
Widespread Support for Voter ID
This is not a partisan issue; it’s a matter of validity and common sense. Poll after poll shows that Californians overwhelmingly support Voter ID requirements:
In January 2026, a Public Opinion Strategies poll showed 79% support for citizenship verification and 68% for voter ID, including 93% of Republicans, 70% of Independents, and 52% of Democrats.
In late April 2025, UC Berkeley IGS Poll found that 71% of registered voters support a proof of citizenship requirement to vote, including 95% of Republicans, 59% of Democrats, and 71% of voters registered with other parties or as “no-party-preference.”
As of March 2026, this Voter ID Initiative has officially turned in more than 1.3 million signatures in all 58 counties in California. With overwhelming support from across the state and data from multiple polls, it’s clear that Voter ID is a unifying, popular solution whose time has come.
Why It Matters – Now
Recent expansions of mail-in voting, automatic registration, and suspension of safeguards have put trust in elections at risk. States with Voter ID laws and citizenship checks tend to enjoy higher public confidence and fewer election disputes. It’s time for California to adopt a system we can trust.
Voter ID does not eliminate mail-in ballots; it updates a system to ensure that each ballot is counted accurately. It gives all California voters an extra layer of trust in the election process.
Californians for Voter ID, Yes on 39

It doesn’t affect voters who changed their names and doesn’t require voters to submit passports, birth certificates, marriage licenses, or citizenship paperwork.
A:
Does Prop 39 suppress votes or prohibit legitimate citizens from voting?
Q:
No. Mail-in voters are only asked to provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID number . This is the same baseline data you are already required to provide when you register to vote, and it does not expose any full ID numbers.
A:
Does writing an ID number on mail-in ballot envelopes risk identity theft?
Q:
No. Prop 39 was placed on the ballot by 1.3 million California citizens . It is an independent, state-focused solution designed to improve public transparency and standard registration maintenance at the local level. There are no ties to federal proposed legislation or politicians.
A:
Is Prop 39 a partisan scheme backed by national politicians?
Q:
No. Modernizing voter-roll systems and cleaning old, inaccurate records can reduce waste from duplicate, outdated, or undeliverable election mail . Independent audits every two years add transparency, accountability, and confidence that election officials are following the law. It does not require voters to provide additional information when registering to vote.
A:
Will citizenship checks create new burdens for voters?
Q:
No. Over 100,000 mail ballots were rejected in 2024 due to signature mismatches . Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-39) would change how Californians verify their identities when voting, replacing signature matching for mail-in ballots with government-issued identification numbers and requiring identification at polling places. Hoover Institution scholar Justin Grimmer examines the proposal, the safeguards already in place, and what research reveals about voter fraud and election security. He also addresses concerns that stricter identification requirements could discourage voting, explaining why studies suggest their effects on turnout and election outcomes are minimal. Grimmer also explores whether Proposition 39 could strengthen public trust in California's elections.
ABOUT THE SERIES
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides) equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.
Launching in advance of the 2026 election, California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides) will answer the questions Californians are already asking (from housing affordability and energy costs to education, public safety, state finances, and election administration) while also explaining how California government works and what the governor, Legislature, and ballot initiatives can and cannot change. More than an election resource, California Decides is intended to become Hoover’s permanent platform for California civic education: a trusted destination where voters, policymakers, journalists, educators, and community leaders can find clear, evidence-based explanations of the state’s most important challenges and the choices that will shape its future.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

Guest Commentary written by Marisol Ramirez Marisol Ramirez is a member of the Inland Empire Latino Giving Circle, advancing democratic participation, community leadership and equitable access to civic institutions. This November, Californians will head to the ballot box and participate in another election with real consequences for our communities. As a Latina and local philanthropist in the Inland Empire who has spent nearly two decades working to strengthen civic participation, I have learned that democracy is strongest when elections are both accessible and secure. From celebrating newly naturalized citizens (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/new-citizen-voting-honor-community/) after they cast their first ballot to watching young people become lifelong voters because someone took the time to explain the process (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2024/09/not-everyone-has-privilege-vote/), I know how important it is for every voter to have the power to decide the future of our country. That progress deserves careful protection, yet it stands in jeopardy this fall. Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), one of the many statewide ballot propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) California voters will tackle, essentially will make it harder for all voters to participate in future elections. If passed, it would require eligible voters to present a government-issued ID for in-person voting. It would also ask mail-in voters to provide the last four digits of a government ID on their ballots, which election officials would need to subsequently verify against their voter registration information. California’s voting law is already clear (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/frequently-asked-questions#voterreg): Any individual who wants to register to vote must state, under penalty of perjury, that they are a United States citizen. That requires everyone to provide information to verify their identity, such as a driver’s license or a social security number. Since California has a process in place to require all potential voters to prove their eligibility, Prop. 39 is a redundant step that will simply add new barriers for voters to cast a ballot. And it is already a federal crime (https://forumtogether.org/article/the-myths-and-truths-of-noncitizen-voting-in-the-united-states/) to vote if you are not a citizen. Should voters pass Prop. 39, millions of Californians could encounter difficulties at the ballot box and could be denied the right to participate in our elections — despite being eligible to vote. Chief among them would be the communities I have worked most closely with: Latinos and young people. Over 1 in 4 Latino adults (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) do not have a driver’s license that shows their current name or address, with 41% of youth, age 18-24, (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%202024%20%281%29.pdf) in a similar predicament. As the political power of Latinos and young people grows with every election cycle, these measures are designed to undercut their influence in California policy and politics for generations to come. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/) Many eligible voters, particularly immigrant and mixed-status communities, already hesitate to engage with government systems out of concern for their privacy and how their personal information is used (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/04/california-dmv-shares-immigrant-driver-data/). Adding a new ID requirement may unintentionally deepen that hesitation, ultimately discouraging civic participation among eligible voters, while raising questions about implementation costs, data security and overall public trust. Proponents argue that presenting ID when voting deters fraud and maintains election integrity, but numerous studies have shown that voter fraud is astoundingly rare. According to the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice, voter fraud incidents have hovered between 0.0003% and 0.0025% (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth), making it virtually nonexistent. To add one final point, instituting more stringent voter identification processes would have major fiscal impacts to California taxpayers. As the state faces ongoing budget deficits, the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026) that creating a brand new form of identification — as Prop. 39 would mandate — could cost anywhere from tens of millions of dollars to the low hundreds of millions. Even if it is supposedly free to obtain, it carries a major price tag. Any reasonable Californian can agree that taxpayer funds should not be wasted on problems that do not exist. California is home to more than 27 million eligible voters (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/154day-primary-2026/complete-ror.pdf), making the state the largest individual democracy in the entire nation. In a moment when the nation is commemorating its 250th anniversary, now is not a time to make it more difficult to participate in our elections. Rather, Californians can live up to the ideals our founding fathers bequeathed to us all by ensuring every eligible Californian can participate confidently, freely and fully. New Analysis: Prop. 39 Would Create New Barriers to Voting for Millions of California Voters
Report Examines How Proposed Requirements Could Make Voting More Difficult, Increase Costs, and Limit Californians’ Say in Policymaking
September 10, 2026 | By Kyra Moeller (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kyra-moeller/)
SACRAMENTO, CA — A new publication (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-39-explained-what-voter-id-would-mean-for-california/) from the California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) (Budget Center) examines Proposition 39, a measure on the November ballot that would establish new voter identification and citizenship verification requirements in California and impose additional responsibilities and costs on state and local election officials.
The analysis finds that Prop. 39 would create unnecessary barriers for millions of eligible California voters, including people who lack an up-to-date driver’s license or other qualifying identification. The measure would also require voters who cast ballots by mail to write the last four digits of a unique identifying number from a government-issued ID on the outside of their ballot envelope, potentially increasing the risk of identity theft. In addition, Prop. 39 would require election officials to use “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of registered voters using government data — a process the report finds could incorrectly flag eligible US citizens and potentially result in voters being removed from the rolls.
“Prop. 39 would impose new and costly requirements on California voters and election officials without actually addressing a real problem,” said Scott Graves, budget director at the California Budget & Policy Center. “California already has in place strong safeguards to verify voter identity and protect the integrity of elections. Adding new requirements would make it harder for eligible Californians to vote while creating new costs for the state.”
The report places Prop. 39 in the broader context of efforts to restrict voting rights and considers what is at stake when barriers to voting limit participation in elections. Voting gives Californians a voice in public policies that affect their lives and communities, including decisions about how public resources are raised and spent. The report highlights the historical connection between democratic participation and taxation and argues that policies that make it harder for people to vote can also limit the ability of communities — particularly young people, people with low incomes, and people of color — to have a say in decisions about public investments and taxes.
“When you make it harder to vote, you make it harder to have fair representation or a say in decisions that shape your community — like how tax dollars get raised and spent,” added Graves.
Who’s At Risk
The report shows that about 2.7 million voting-age Californians who are US citizens do not have a driver’s license , while more than 3 million have a driver’s license that is expired, from another state, or lacks updated information. Nearly one-quarter of voting-age Californians without a driver’s license also lack a California state ID card. The measure could disproportionately affect people of color, young people, people with lower incomes, and people with disabilities, who are less likely to have a driver’s license. Prop. 39 would also impose substantial costs on state and local governments, with the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimating annual costs could range from tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars. The measure provides no new revenue to pay for these expenses.
The analysis also finds that Prop. 39’s citizenship verification requirements could incorrectly flag eligible US citizens due to errors, inconsistencies, and outdated information in government databases. Voters whose citizenship is mistakenly called into question could face burdensome processes to correct their records and could potentially lose their ability to vote if they fail to resolve the issue before an election. More broadly, requiring identifying information on ballot envelopes could increase the risk of identity theft and potentially discourage Californians from using the state’s most common method of voting.
Rather than creating additional barriers to voting, the report identifies ways California can strengthen voter participation and improve the election process. These include exploring options for moving toward automatic voter registration, providing dedicated funding for voter outreach and engagement, supporting civic education, and investing in county election offices and systems that could help accelerate ballot counting while maintaining election security and voter access.
California voters will decide on Proposition 39 in November. The Budget Center’s analysis provides information on the measure’s proposed requirements, potential impacts, and fiscal implications to help Californians understand the choices before them.
To view the full publication and additional analyses, visit www.calbudgetcenter.org/resources/ (http://www.calbudgetcenter.org/resources/) .

Endorsement: Prop 39 would create CEQA for voting rights. No thanks
Even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California (it’s not), Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit
Proposition 39 would require Californians to present or incorporate some form of identification when voting. It is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters. The Chronicle’s editorial board recommends a no vote.
Todd Trumbull/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 12, 2026
Is voter fraud rampant in California?
A May poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California) found that 41% of likely voters here were either “very” or “somewhat” concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible voters to cast ballots.
That’s not an insignificant number.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.

California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).

# Strict Voter Identification Laws, Turnout, and Election Outcomes
Mark Hoekstra & Vijetha Koppa
Working Paper 26206
DOI 10.3386/w26206
Issue Date August 2019
Since 2000, ten states have enacted strict voter identification laws, which require that voters show identification in order for their votes to count.
While proponents argue these laws prevent voter fraud and protect the integrity of elections, opponents argue they disenfranchise low-income and minority voters.
In this paper, we document the extent to which these laws can affect voter turnout and election outcomes.
We do so using historical data on more than 2,000 races in Florida and Michigan, which both allow and track ballots cast without identification.
Results indicate that at most only 0.10% and 0.31% of total votes cast in each state were cast without IDs.
Thus, even under the extreme assumption that all voters without IDs were either fraudulent or would be disenfranchised by a strict law, the enactment of such a law would have only a very small effect on turnout.
Similarly, we also show under a range of conservative assumptions that very few election results could have been flipped due to a strict law.
Collectively, our findings indicate that even if the worst fears of proponents or critics were true, strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.

# Voter ID laws aren’t worth fighting over
Which is just what researchers Vincent Pons and Enrico Cantoni found when they analyzed the impact, across multiple states and election cycles, of enacting rules requiring citizens to show ID before voting.
The effects of voter ID laws are “mostly null,” they conclude in a paper for the National Bureau of Economic Research.
“Strict ID laws have no significant negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any subgroup defined by age, gender, race, or party affiliation.
Most importantly, they do not decrease the participation of ethnic minorities relative to whites.
The laws’ overall effects remain close to zero.”
At the same time, Pons and Cantoni found no evidence that voter ID requirements have a significant impact on voter fraud or on public confidence in the integrity of elections.
In states where ID laws have been adopted, there has been no increase in either the number of fraud cases or their likelihood of being reported.
Nor has there been any perceptible increase in other kinds of political participation.

# California Trusted Information
### Reality: Voting by mail is a reliable and secure way to vote.
**Rumor:** Vote by mail is being forced on voters and the mail in ballots are susceptible to fraud.
**Facts:** Mail in ballots provide more security to elections, not less.
Elections officials use protocols to verify the eligibility and identity of the voter prior to sending the vote by mail ballot.
When the ballot is returned elections officials will verify the voter’s identity through signature verification.
If the elections official determines that the voter's signature does not match, the identification envelope will not be opened, and the ballot will not be counted until the identification of the voter is confirmed.
If a voter loses, fails to receive, or makes a mistake on their ballot, they can request another vote by mail ballot from their county elections official or go to a polling place to receive a replacement ballot.
We take voter fraud allegations seriously and will investigate each claim.
Information about specific voter fraud should be detailed in a complaint to our office, which can be completed online via our Election Voter Complaint form.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: October 15, 2026 at 3:13 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
A healthy democracy depends on both public participation and public trust. Without either, the system risks disaffection and loss of legitimacy.
California has made numerous moves in recent years to boost voter participation. From making it easier than ever to vote by mail to overly-liberal ballot harvesting laws, the Golden State has worked to optimize the public participation component of its election administration.
California has also maintained rising levels of public confidence in aspects of its elections. In 2017, just 47% of likely voters and 40% of adults either had “quite a lot of” or a “great deal of” confidence in how California counts votes, according to surveys by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California. By 2024, those figures rose to 63% and 53%, respectively.
Lurking beneath (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/time-trends-all-adults-1024-corrected.pdf) those 2024 numbers were bigger concerns about election integrity than those figures suggest. The same survey found that 42% of adults and 43% of likely voters said they were “somewhat concerned” or “very concerned” that it’s “too easy for people who are not eligible to vote in California elections.”
Enter Proposition 39.
The proposal seeks to improve public confidence in elections with a simple rule: voters must present a government-issued ID when voting in person or include the last four digits of a government-issued ID that corresponds to identification used at the time of registration on the ballots they intend to mail in. For those who do not have such identification, the measure calls for free identification to be provided for voting.
It also requires election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists and “use best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations. Finally, it directs regular audits by the State Auditor to ensure compliance with these rules and offer recommendations for how to improve election integrity.
There’s nothing radical about these recommendations. Thirty six states require voters to present some form of identification when voting. Such a requirement is commonplace around the world, including in Canada and Mexico. The logic of identification requirements is quite obvious: it’s simply another check to ensure that people are who they say they are when they vote. In fact, poll workers in California already ask (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/trusted-info-voter-id-reg-requirements.pdf) first-time federal election voters who didn’t include an ID number at the time of registration for ID if they show up to the polls.
Opponents of voter identification requirements counter that requiring voters to provide identification at the polls is an unacceptable barrier to democratic participation. We disagree. If people can clear the “barrier” of presenting an ID to buy cigarettes or alcohol or use a credit card or get on an airplane, they can present ID to vote.
Opponents likewise counter that requiring voters to write the last four digits of their ID on their ballots introduces a failure point or privacy risk. We are sympathetic to privacy concerns, though such concerns would be more serious if the rule was to write the total ID number. And the failure point is real — what if voters write the wrong numbers? — but fixable. Ballots can be cured.
Research on the impact of such rules has been mixed over the years, with one review published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2019 finding (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) that “strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.” Echoing this is an analysis published (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) by the journal Research & Politics in December 2024 which found “no compelling evidence that strict voter ID laws consistently suppress or boost voter turnout. Rather, the modest and opposing impacts across contexts appear to net out to minimal aggregate effects on participation, consistent with research showing that electoral reforms often produce small equilibrium effects.”

What could be the most controversial component of the measure is its mandate that election officials use “best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations using “government data.” The measure does not define these terms, thus giving the state and election officials room to figure out how to do that in the most reasonable manner possible. While this editorial board isn’t of the view that noncitizen voting is rampant, it doesn’t seem irrational to occasionally confirm people who attest to their citizenship actually are citizens.
If passed, we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period as it’s worked out. Combining the convenience of voting with basic verification isn’t voter suppression — it’s just common-sense governance. Vote Yes on Proposition 39.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:04 PM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.

Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.

The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.

“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.

“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.

“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.
